headline: Christofi argues recent weak clearance rates and cautious investor sentiment create a contrarian buying opportunity in Australian residential property right now.
reasoning: Christofi invokes the classic contrarian maxim — be greedy when others are fearful — to argue that current market hesitancy is creating better negotiating conditions, improved terms, and good entry prices for buyers. He warns that waiting for the dust to settle leads to paralysis by analysis and that the long-term case for affordable residential property remains intact. He notes that the two constants — aging population and ongoing tax obligations — mean retirement shortfalls will perpetuate demand for income-producing property.
quote: When when people are fearful, be greedy. When people are greedy, be fearful. So now's the time you will get good opportunities. So when you're seeing the clearance rates are not so high, you'll tend to see you'll get better negotiation deals, better terms.

headline: Chris Christofi highlights builder financial due diligence as the critical risk-management step when investing in new residential property, noting early warning signs before builder insolvency.
reasoning: Christofi stresses the importance of checking builder financials, payment histories, and build quality as early warning indicators of financial distress before a builder goes bust. He notes that even well-known strong builders have collapsed, but that signs typically precede failure — such as cutting corners on fixtures or delays in completing bills. Reventon has experienced roughly 15–20 builder failures across 3,700 sales and in each case was able to appoint a replacement builder or address the issue at land stage.
quote: Strong financials, proven track record. Now, you mentioned the very, very good point. You had some of the strongest ones very well known, which I don't like to mention names on online go down. And so it can happen to anyone. But all we can do is put as many checks and balances in place. Look at their financials. Look if their payments have all been on time. Look at their bills. Look at if they're completing their bills on time. Because usually what happens is before a builder goes bus there's usually signs. Now they're cutting corners. When they're completing the project they're not putting the same fixtures and fittings or they're not putting the same care.

headline: Reventon's Chris Christofi argues Australian property market weakness is concentrated at the top end, with affordable housing remaining resilient due to persistent supply-demand imbalance.
reasoning: Christofi contends that negative media headlines about property are misleading because they reflect weakness primarily in the $2–$9 million segment. Affordable housing, which he defines as his speciality, continues to grow with high demand driven by rental need, tax incentives on new builds, and structural undersupply. He argues that supply-demand imbalance, infrastructure investment, and affordability metrics remain the core underpinnings of real estate value and that these factors remain intact at the lower end of the market.
quote: A lot of people are worried about headlines, but there's so many things that underpin real estate. It's not just 1 or 2. Supply and demand, you know, infrastructure affordable. We've got a, you know, crisis in affordable housing. All these things underpin real estate. So although some areas of the market have taken a big hit, predominantly the two to the $9 million mark, affordable real estate, which is what I specialize in, is still growing and it still has very high demand because so many people need to rent their property, they need to start investing for their future.
episode_title: Where are the next property hotspots?

headline: Chris Christofi urges property investors to act now while clearance rates are low and negotiating conditions are favourable rather than waiting for the dust to settle.
reasoning: Christofi argues that the current environment of lower clearance rates and negative media sentiment is precisely the time to act, drawing on the classic contrarian adage of being greedy when others are fearful. He warns that paralysis by analysis causes investors to defer action by one, two or three years, compounding their retirement shortfall. Smart money is already moving and better negotiation terms and deals are available now for those willing to act.
quote: All this negative media and people are waiting for the dust to settle. But it's a very, very common adage, you know, when when people are fearful, be greedy. When people are greedy, be fearful. So now's the time you will get good opportunities. So when you're seeing the clearance rates are not so high, you'll tend to see you'll get better negotiation deals, better terms. So now smart money's moving. Now people are active. And I beg people to make sure that they still take action and not sit on the fence because one tenth, one year turns into two years, 10 to 3 years, and then you've got a bigger shortfall in retirement.

headline: Uses a 'property clock' framework to identify emerging growth areas nationwide, targeting markets at the 9 o'clock position before they peak.
reasoning: Christofi describes a systematic rotation across Australian states following the property clock cycle, having moved through regional Victoria, south-east Queensland, Adelaide, Perth, and Tasmania over the past decade-plus. He argues it is critical to take a nationwide view rather than focusing on a single state, and to identify forward indicators — infrastructure spend and affordability — in areas 2–3 years before they peak. Entering a market already widely recognised as growing means missing the early heavy-lifting phase of appreciation.
quote: If you look at the property clock and the property cycle in that real estate that I've been selling since 2012, we went from regional Victoria, south east Queensland, Adelaide, Perth, Tasmania, and every 2 or 3 years we're looking at that new area that's going to grow, that's showing all those forward indicators. If you're talking about an area that's growing, you're probably lost that peak where it's going to really grow in the first few years and do the heavy lifting.
episode_title: Where are the next property hotspots?
